```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Willingness to pay is better documented and much higher in A. Pricing pages from Canny, Frill, Featul and Userback, plus a 62-tool pricing study, show paid entry plans at about $25-$31/mo, scaling to $79-$349/mo. B's anchor is $4-7/mo, and one of B's own demand quotes says users want it free because 'caregivers are usually financially stressed.'",
    "A's buyer is a B2B SaaS team spending from a software budget. That is a more reliable source of one paying customer in 90 days than B's financially stressed consumer caregiver, who must also recruit siblings for the product to work.",
    "B has structural revenue problems that A lacks. Customer lifetime is naturally capped when the parent moves to facility care or dies. Multi-sibling adoption is a documented activation hurdle. Both make sub-$10/mo pricing fragile for a solo operator.",
    "B's regulatory exposure is heavier for a one-person shop. It handles consumer health data that may fall under the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, and Washington's My Health My Data Act carries a private right of action. A's GDPR/CCPA obligations (DPA, privacy policy, records of processing) are standard and mostly one-time drafting.",
    "Both markets are crowded: 73 tools in A versus 6+ live direct competitors in B. Crowding therefore does not separate them. A's higher revenue per customer gives more room to absorb its higher acquisition costs ($5.42 Google CPC)."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's main paid acquisition channel is backed only by a 2017 WordStream Facebook CPC benchmark (~$1-3). It is about nine years old and not specific to caregivers, so it says little about current CAC for sandwich-generation targeting. B's partner-channel cost is also inferred from a different company's referral program (CareStitch), not tested. B's case-for claim that SplitKin, TendTo and CircleCare are one- or two-person teams has no source and counts as missing.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. Both briefs describe saturated categories, and neither shows achievable CAC against LTV. A's direct demand evidence is thin: two quotes, one of which complains that $50-80/mo is too expensive. Its marketing source warns that generic feedback tools get ignored. A wins mainly on payer quality and price point, not on stronger proof of demand or a clear wedge."
}
```
